includedSources.name: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom

items.title: A 'typical' tightening cycle at 3%+ inflation ends near 6%, not the 4.75% the curve prices
items.idea: Fed funds is 4% and priced to top at 4.75%, but Podolsky argues a normal tightening cycle with inflation stuck above 3% would take it closer to 6%. Same in Japan: the market sees a 2% terminal, versus ~4% as the 'normal' policy rate before Japan's deflation era. He calls Waller's 50bp idea appropriate and says the Fed is 'well behind the curve.' The US and Japan are both seeing the inflation impulse; other countries much less so.
items.angle: If terminal is 125bp too low, the repricing lands in the 2s and in USD/JPY carry, not just equities. The US+Japan pairing is the unusual part: the two biggest sovereign debtors repricing together is the term-premium story.
items.tweetA: Curve says the Fed tops at 4.75%. History says hiking cycles with inflation above 3% end nearer 6%. That gap is 125bp of repricing nobody has positioned for. $TLT $SHY
items.tweetB: US and Japan are the two countries where inflation won't die, and they're also the two biggest sovereign debt stacks in the G7. Not a coincidence. Rising nominal growth in a fiscal-dominance world just looks like this. $JGB $USDJPY

charts.desc: US vs Japan inflation (Bloomberg); further charts in the full letter.

items.title: Nvidia's $530B in commitments is roughly the Tier 1 capital of the largest US banks
items.idea: WSJ puts Nvidia's total commitments at $530B. Podolsky says that's about the Tier 1 capital of the biggest US banks combined, and banks lever capital ~10:1, so every dollar of credit underwrites about $10 of demand. His guess is that the new leadership shuts that lending down, which is bearish for AI demand at the margin.
items.angle: This is the clearest way to frame the 'Bank of Nvidia' risk: it's not about who replaces Jensen, it's about how much demand gets withdrawn if Nvidia stops lending. Watch neocloud credit ($CRWV bonds) before you watch $NVDA guidance.
items.tweetA: $530B of Nvidia commitments is about the Tier 1 capital of America's biggest banks. Now picture that bank getting a new chair whose first instinct is to cut the loan book. $NVDA $CRWV
items.tweetB: Everyone is asking who the next Nvidia CEO will be. Wrong question. The real one: how much 2027 GPU demand was underwritten by Nvidia's own balance sheet, and what happens when the CFO now in charge stops writing guarantees?

items.title: Inflation politics: hawkish shading plus local permitting is how data center growth gets slowed
items.idea: Voters everywhere hate inflation. Podolsky argues Democrats know they can't be tied to inflation and win the presidency in 2028, and that unelected Fed officials still read public anger, so policy will lean toward fighting inflation. Data center growth is largely regulated locally, which makes it an easy political target for higher power bills and higher rates.
items.angle: Pair this with the Boebert flip and the 'race to close deals before Democrats return' talk (TWiST). The political cost of AI capex (power prices, land use) is becoming a 2028 campaign issue, which is a slow-moving risk for $VST, $CEG and hyperscaler capex.
items.tweetA: The AI buildout has two political enemies now: voters who hate inflation, and county boards that approve data centers. Both get louder in 2028. Capex models don't price permitting risk.
items.tweetB: If inflation is the issue that decides 2028, the electricity bill is the most visible inflation there is, and data centers are the easiest thing to blame. Nobody is ready for 'AI is raising your power bill' as a campaign slogan.

items.title: Absorption ceiling: even a small, bureaucracy-free firm can't use new models as fast as they ship
items.idea: Podolsky notes that AI is woven into many processes at Kate Capital, a small firm with no bureaucracy, and they still can't take on new models fast enough. 'Most of us probably don't need better models.' The constraint is moving from model capability to how fast organizations can absorb it.
items.angle: If adoption speed, not intelligence, is the binding constraint, value moves to integration and workflow layers (agents, Duet-style tools) and away from frontier model pricing power. That bears directly on Anthropic IPO multiples.
items.tweetA: A macro PM says his tiny, bureaucracy-free firm can't keep up with new AI models. If the most agile users are already saturated, the frontier labs' pricing power depends on enterprises that move ten times slower.
items.tweetB: Model progress is exponential, but organizational absorption isn't. The gap between the two is where the next decade of AI services revenue lives, and it's not at the model layer.

items.title: The rare regime where neither stocks nor bonds work
items.idea: In good times you're long both stocks and bonds and make money; usually at least the combination works. Podolsky argues central banks need to tighten significantly while equity prices still assume a continued boom, which leaves an environment where neither asset works. He adds that Anthropic IPOs next week 'oversubscribed', will likely be cash-flow negative for years, and has tens of billions of shares eligible for sale on Thursday: 'If the stock starts to trade down, that's a sign.'
items.angle: Capital Flows says the same thing from a different angle: more than half of 60/40's nominal return has been eaten by inflation, like 2022. Two independent sources calling a correlation-breakdown regime means looking at real assets, short-duration and trend.
items.tweetA: Stocks priced for a boom. Bonds priced for disinflation. A Fed that has to disappoint one of them, probably both. 2022 was the last time 60/40 had no hiding place.
items.tweetB: Podolsky's tell for next week: if Anthropic trades down after an 'oversubscribed' IPO with tens of billions of shares unlocked, that's the market telling you the AI risk premium has reset. One print, a lot of information.

items.title: Claims still at 200k while ZipRecruiter says 'growing again' in a low-hire, low-fire market
items.idea: Initial claims rose 9k to 200k (6k above estimates) but the 4-week average stayed at 195k; continuing claims fell to 1.697mm from 1.717mm. ZipRecruiter: 'we are growing again despite a low hire, low fire market.'
items.angle: Falling continuing claims undercut the 'slowdown' story Tavi Costa is flagging in industrials. Labor is giving the Fed no reason to stop hiking, which supports the front-end-short view.
items.tweetA: Continuing claims are falling, not rising. Initial claims at 200k. If you're waiting for the labor market to bail out the Fed, it isn't coming. $ZIP
items.tweetB: A hiring marketplace saying 'we're growing again' is a better leading signal than any survey. Low-fire labor markets mean the Fed can keep hiking without a body count, until it suddenly can't.

items.title: Mortgage rates fall a 4th straight week to 7.21%; purchase apps jump 7.5%
items.idea: Average mortgage rates fell for a 4th straight week to 7.21%, purchase applications rebounded 7.5% w/w and refis rose 4.5%. Separately, Ferguson cites 'ongoing weak new residential construction.'
items.angle: Housing demand is highly sensitive to even 20-30bp moves at a 7%+ level. If the 2Y keeps selling off on Fed hikes, this small bounce reverses; watch the 10Y mortgage spread.
items.tweetA: Mortgage rates down four weeks in a row and purchase apps jump 7.5%. That's how pent-up housing demand is: a small rate dip and buyers show up. Now the Fed wants to hike 50bp. $XHB $ITB
items.tweetB: Ferguson says new residential construction is still weak while mortgage apps rebound. Demand is there and supply isn't getting built. That's a sticky shelter inflation setup for 2027.

items.title: CoreWeave and Nebius: old GPU fleets re-contracting at premiums, customers prepaying more
items.idea: CoreWeave: the original fleet is 're-contracting at premiums,' producing cash flow above what was assumed, and the newest contracts are 'among the most profitable we have ever underwritten.' Nebius: customers are committing 'for longer, at higher prices, and they are paying more upfront. Prices keep rising.'
items.angle: This goes straight at the GPU-depreciation bear case: if older GPUs re-price up at renewal, useful-life assumptions are conservative. That's the opposite of the 'GPUs are melting' narrative, the same week Nvidia's financing machine is being questioned.
items.tweetA: The bear case on neoclouds was that old GPUs become worthless. CoreWeave says its original fleet is re-contracting at a PREMIUM. If true, the depreciation debate is backwards. $CRWV $NBIS
items.tweetB: Customers paying more upfront for longer contracts at higher prices sounds like a seller's market in compute. Meanwhile $NVDA is down 14% this week. Either the end market or the stock is wrong.

items.title: Cisco says 'early in the networking super cycle'; Legence says data center builds continue post-election
items.idea: Cisco: strong start to FY27 shows 'the criticality of networking and security together as agentic AI accelerates... we are still early in the networking super cycle,' with enterprise adoption just beginning. Legence: data center customers say after the election they are continuing their plans to build.
items.angle: Post-election continuity on builds matters given the political risk Podolsky raises. The enterprise networking leg ($CSCO, $ANET) is less exposed to the Nvidia financing question than GPU clouds.
items.tweetA: Data center contractors say post-election customers aren't changing build plans. Cisco says enterprise AI networking is 'just beginning.' The AI trade isn't over; it's rotating away from the one company everyone owns. $CSCO $LGN
items.tweetB: Agentic AI needs more east-west traffic and more security inspection per request. If that's right, networking capex grows faster than compute capex in the next phase. $ANET $CSCO

items.title: Plumbers and engines: Ferguson commercial/mechanical +17% and Cummins power gen point to data center demand
items.idea: Ferguson's commercial/mechanical business rose 17%, driven by large capital projects (data centers, pharma, biotech, general manufacturing) that offset weak resi. Cummins cites 'continued strength in global power generation, particularly from data center customers,' plus better North American heavy and medium-duty truck demand.
items.angle: The second-derivative AI suppliers (pipes, gensets) are posting real numbers. If the Nvidia financing loop tightens, these lag, but their order books are 12-24 months long, giving a buffer.
items.tweetA: Ferguson +17% in commercial/mechanical. Cummins power gen driven by data centers. The AI boom shows up in pipe, valves and diesel gensets well before it shows up in GDP. $FERG $CMI
items.tweetB: Pharma reshoring and data centers are now the same trade for industrial distributors. One is policy-driven, one is capex-driven, and they rarely both stop at once. $FERG

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: Semis -4.5% on a soft PPI day; Nvidia -14% w/w and ~$2T lost since October, yet SPX only ~3% off its high
items.idea: Friday: chip sector -4.5%, NDX -1.5% at worst, NVDA -14% since the prior Friday (worst week since April 2025), BTC below $70k, all on a softer-than-expected PPI that should have helped. NVDA has lost nearly $2T in market cap since its October peak while SPX sits only ~3% below its record, propped up by rotation into healthcare, staples and selected chip competitors.
items.angle: When good macro news can't lift the leader, it's distribution. Daily Chartbook's stat backs this up: every prior SMH -25% / XLK -15% episode had SPY in a double-digit drawdown. The index is either late or it's a real rotation.
items.tweetA: Soft PPI. Front end rallies. Semis -4.5% anyway. When a market won't rally on the news it needs, someone large is getting out. $SMH $NVDA
items.tweetB: $2T of Nvidia market cap gone since October and the S&P is 3% off its high. That's either the healthiest rotation in years or an index that hasn't caught up to its own leadership yet. $SPY $XLV $XLP

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: Bessent publicly blames Commerce: Treasury, USTR and State backed listing Megaspeed for months
items.idea: Treasury Secretary Bessent said Treasury, USTR and State supported putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce held the authority. Lutnick is reportedly marginalized. Innes's view: the Washington blame game could be more disruptive than the corporate scandal, through tighter export rules, more customer investigations and scrutiny of overseas data-center arrangements.
items.angle: Political risk now spreads to every overseas GPU deployment (Malaysia, Gulf). Gulf AI campus deals and neocloud contracts in Southeast Asia face new diligence risk.
items.tweetA: A sitting Treasury Secretary publicly saying 'Commerce had the pen' on Megaspeed is a cabinet fight in the open. The policy result is almost always tighter rules, not looser. $NVDA $SMCI
items.tweetB: The next leg of export controls won't target chips going to China. It will target where chips are INSTALLED: Malaysia, Singapore, the Gulf. Every overseas data center contract just picked up a new risk factor.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: Hyperscalers fund AI from cash flow; neoclouds fund it from lenders, and rates decide which survives
items.idea: CoreWeave rebounded midweek on strong Q3 and guidance pointing to profitability in H1 2028, then gave the gains back as its dependence on the Nvidia ecosystem returned to focus. Innes: the strategy works only if customers stay committed, the chips keep their economic value, and financing stays available, and all three get harder as rates rise. 'The income statement can look like a champagne reception while the balance sheet resembles the morning after.'
items.angle: Profitability in H1 2028 means 18+ months of refinancing risk in a hiking cycle. The spread between hyperscaler and neocloud credit is the cleanest expression of this view.
items.tweetA: CoreWeave's profitability target is H1 2028. That's six more quarters of needing lenders in a market where the Fed is talking 50bp hikes. Duration risk isn't only in bonds. $CRWV
items.tweetB: Microsoft funds AI capex from free cash flow. CoreWeave funds it from creditors. Same trade, completely different risk. If you're long AI infra, your capital structure choice matters more than the stock you pick.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: From cuts to a jumbo hike in under a year: CPI +0.4/+0.3, DXY at a 19-month high, PPI soft in the details
items.idea: October CPI: headline +0.4%, core +0.3%. Waller floated a 50bp December hike, sending short yields sharply higher and the dollar to a ~19-month high. Annual PPI inflation hit its fastest since 2022 but came in slightly below estimates, with softer PCE-feeding components. Innes still expects a 25bp hike in December, arguing the market priced the threat, not the outcome.
items.angle: If PCE components are soft, the 50bp tail is overpriced. A 25bp December hike would be a relief rally for the front end, so fading the 50bp odds is a tactical trade.
items.tweetA: Waller went from talking cuts to talking a 50bp hike in under a year. That's not forward guidance, that's a U-turn. The dollar at a 19-month high is the market believing him. $DXY
items.tweetB: Annual PPI is the hottest since 2022, but the PCE-relevant pieces came in soft. The market priced the 50bp threat this week; the Fed probably delivers 25. That gap is the trade.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: Crude -18% from peak on 'deal' hopes while tankers are still being hit around Hormuz
items.idea: Crude is ~18% off its peak as markets weigh a possible US-Iran arrangement; Brent recovered toward $96 and talk of a supply surplus is growing. But tankers are still being struck or disabled around Hormuz, regional infrastructure is vulnerable, and the lull in fighting isn't a peace deal. 'Oil remains the truth serum of the macro market.'
items.angle: Commodity Context sees the same split: speculative Brent length at its lowest since July while physical stocks remain extremely low. Positioning is light into a headline-sensitive tape, so upside risk is asymmetric.
items.tweetA: Oil is 18% off its high because of a deal that doesn't exist, while tankers are still getting hit in Hormuz. Pricing a ceasefire as a treaty has never ended well. $USO $XLE
items.tweetB: Lower oil is the only thing that gives the Fed room to slow down. So the Fed's December decision partly depends on Hormuz. Rates traders have become oil traders whether they like it or not.

items.source: Stephen Innes / The Dark Side Of The Boom
items.title: Next week's dual test: Nvidia earnings (Nov 17) and the Anthropic IPO answer different questions
items.idea: Interim CEO Colette Kress reports on Nov 17 and has to show the machine runs without the man who built it over 33 years; Innes says to watch strategic investments, customer commitments and Nvidia's role financing the ecosystem, more than revenue. Anthropic's IPO prices the next generation of AI growth; Nvidia's call tests confidence in the machinery behind the current one.
items.angle: The key line in the Nvidia call is any change to guarantees or strategic investments policy. A cut there is bearish for neoclouds even if the revenue beat is huge.
items.tweetA: Nvidia will beat on revenue Tuesday. That isn't the number that matters. The number is how many backstops and guarantees Kress plans to roll over. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Same week: Nvidia without its founder reports, Anthropic with its founders lists. The market will price the AI stack's top and bottom at once. Rare to get that clean a read.

items.title: Nominal demand ~6% against a 4% policy rate is an amplifier, not a brake
items.idea: Capital Flows: headline and core inflation are rising together. Nominal demand running near 6% against a 4% policy rate is still stimulative. The inflation swaps market is pricing a slowdown the data doesn't support, and term premium plus the short end point to another leg higher in rates.
items.angle: Policy rate below nominal growth means policy isn't restrictive, which agrees with Podolsky's ~6% terminal argument. Short inflation swaps / long breakevens looks like the mispriced leg.
items.tweetA: Policy rate 4%. Nominal GDP growth ~6%. Until those cross, the Fed isn't tight. It's just less loose. Inflation swaps haven't figured that out yet. $TIP
items.tweetB: Two separate macro shops this week: one says a typical cycle ends near 6%, the other says nominal demand is running near 6%. When different methods land on the same number, take it seriously.

charts.desc: Slide deck and 60/40 study PDFs behind paywall. Charts inside, worth opening.

items.title: More than half of 60/40's nominal return this year has been eaten by inflation, the same setup that came before 2022
items.idea: Capital Flows' 60/40 purchasing-power study: over half of this year's nominal 60/40 return has gone to inflation, which is 'exactly the setup that preceded 2022.' Factor flows show equities positioned for AI momentum, not macro risk.
items.angle: Equities positioned for AI momentum just took a 14% hit in $NVDA. If the momentum factor unwinds while bonds sell off, 2022-style correlation returns.
items.tweetA: Half your 60/40 return this year went to inflation. The last time real returns looked like that was right before 2022, when stocks and bonds fell together. $AOR $SPY $AGG
items.tweetB: Factor flows: equities positioned for AI momentum, not macro risk. That's fine until the AI leader has its worst week since April 2025 and the Fed floats 50bp in the same week. Guess which week this was.

charts.desc: 60/40 purchasing power study PDF. Worth opening.

items.title: Brent briefly breaks $90 for the first time since August, then round-trips; Brent CFDs in contango
items.idea: Brent fell ~$2 on the week to ~$96 after briefly dipping below $90, the first time since August, amid scuttled US diplomacy and Trump signalling a preference for the rocky status quo. Futures curves are still backwardated, but the Brent CFD curve weakened into broader contango, 'the most bearish physical market indicator.'
items.angle: Physical (CFDs) is softer than futures. That's the one to watch: if CFD contango spreads to the prompt futures spread, the deal-hope selloff gets confirmation.
items.tweetA: Brent dipped under $90 for the first time since August and ended the week at $96. A $6 intraweek round trip with the curve still backwardated tells you no one trusts either the deal or the war. $BNO
items.tweetB: Futures are backwardated, physical CFDs are in contango. When paper and physical disagree, physical usually wins. That's the oil chart to watch next week.

charts.desc: Free weekly chart: Brent flat price and timespreads; full deck with inventories and cracks is paid.

items.title: One of the biggest weekly crude builds since the Iran War started, from extremely low levels
items.idea: Inflows hit all major tracked storage hubs. Combined, it's one of the largest weekly stock builds since the start of the Iran War, but stock levels are still 'extremely low.' The IEA now sees the market flipping to a notable supply surplus in October, and Hormuz flows are starting to fall back from their peak wartime level.
items.angle: A build from very low levels is a rate-of-change signal, not a level signal. It supports the bear story without removing the shock risk if Hormuz flows fall again.
items.tweetA: One of the largest crude builds since the war started, and inventories are still extremely low. Bears get the headline, bulls keep the level. $USO
items.tweetB: IEA says surplus in October. Hormuz flows are already slipping from their wartime peak. If both are true, a surplus forecast resting on the Strait staying open is a fragile surplus.

items.title: Gasoline cracks fall below 2025 levels while diesel cracks hold above $80/bbl
items.idea: Refined products are sharply split. Gasoline cracks fell below 2025 levels as US gasoline stocks rose above year-ago levels, while diesel cracks stay above $80/bbl in a tight ~$5 range month-to-date, with diesel stocks low at every tracked hub. Asia's diesel inventories are the least depressed relative to seasonal norms.
items.angle: $80 diesel cracks are an industrial and freight cost, tying into Cummins truck demand and the 'expensive energy' backdrop Innes mentions. Refiners with distillate-heavy yields benefit.
items.tweetA: Gasoline cracks below 2025 levels. Diesel cracks above $80/bbl. Consumers get relief at the pump; truckers, farmers and factories don't. Diesel is the inflation input nobody is watching. $VLO $MPC $PBF
items.tweetB: Diesel at an $80 crack in a supposedly softening oil market says the shortage is in the middle of the barrel, not in crude. Distillate-heavy refiners are running a different business from the crude tape.

items.title: Managed money in ICE Brent drops to its lowest since early July, when the post-MOU rout was still underway
items.idea: ICE data show another heavy round of speculative selling in Brent through Tuesday, taking net managed-money positioning to its lowest since the first week of July. CFTC data are delayed to Monday because of Veterans Day.
items.angle: Light spec positioning plus low inventories plus an unresolved war gives an asymmetric upside skew. A squeeze trigger would be any tanker incident or diplomatic breakdown.
items.tweetA: Speculators are the shortest on Brent since July. Inventories are still extremely low. The war isn't over. That's a coiled spring, not a bear market. $BNO $XLE
items.tweetB: Specs dumped Brent this week on deal hopes, and Trump says he prefers the status quo. Positioning is set up for peace while policy is set up for neither peace nor war.

items.title: Nvidia's checkbook: stakes in 229 private companies plus billions in lease guarantees
items.idea: Per the NYT, Nvidia held stakes in 229 private companies at the end of July and has offered billions in lease guarantees and backstops to start-ups and AI clouds. Axios: the AI boom relies less on Nvidia's chips than a year ago but still depends on its checkbook.
items.angle: 229 private stakes amounts to a venture portfolio. If the new leadership slows new checks, late-stage AI funding rounds (and their valuations) lose a price-insensitive buyer.
items.tweetA: Nvidia owns stakes in 229 private companies. That's not a strategic portfolio, that's a top-10 VC firm that also sells its LPs the picks and shovels. The VC market just lost its least price-sensitive investor.
items.tweetB: 'Less reliant on Nvidia's chips, still dependent on its checkbook.' That sums up the post-Jensen AI economy in eight words. Custom silicon won the chip war; Nvidia won the financing war. Only one of those wins survives a CFO-CEO.

items.title: Interim CEO Kress already halved Nvidia's biggest OpenAI backstop after Jensen belittled her in August
items.idea: WSJ: in an August meeting, Jensen belittled Colette Kress as she pushed back on billions in guarantees to companies that couldn't afford Nvidia's chips. She later cut Nvidia's biggest backstop for OpenAI in half. The Information: Kress has tried to rein in Nvidia's riskiest bets, so the backstop role may contract.
items.angle: The person now running Nvidia is on record as skeptical of the vendor-financing model. That points toward fewer guarantees in 2027, which pressures OpenAI's compute plan and neocloud contracts.
items.tweetA: The new interim CEO of Nvidia is the executive who got belittled for pushing back on guarantees to customers who couldn't afford the chips, and who then cut the OpenAI backstop in half. Policy just changed. $NVDA
items.tweetB: OpenAI's compute plan was built on a supplier willing to guarantee its own sales. That supplier is now run by the person who thought it was a bad idea. Watch OpenAI's next capacity announcement.

items.title: $140B of dealmaking in two months, and the 'Nvidia always steps in' assumption is gone
items.idea: The Information: about $140B of Nvidia dealmaking, including credit guarantees, in just two months this year; the assumption that Nvidia would always step in 'has largely evaporated.' SemiAnalysis: $530B of off-balance-sheet commitments and guarantees, and founder-style bets that rarely survive professional managers.
items.angle: $140B in two months is a run rate of ~$840B a year. Even a partial pullback is a big demand hole for 2027. Price this into neocloud equity and HY spreads.
items.tweetA: $140B of Nvidia deals in two months annualizes to ~$840B. That's more than most countries' annual capex. The 'Nvidia put' under AI demand is being repriced in real time.
items.tweetB: 'Founder-style bets rarely survive professional managers.' That's SemiAnalysis on Nvidia. It's also the history of almost every founder-led capex cycle. Finance-run companies don't guarantee their customers' leases.

items.title: 11 names, six months, no dual-class shield: why Nvidia's board could act and Meta's couldn't
items.idea: Axios lists 11 succession candidates, from Kress and CUDA's Ian Buck inside to Rene Haas (approached, per FT), Lisa Su and Johny Srouji outside, with Tim Cook and Madison Huang as long shots. The search could take six months. Unlike other founder-scandal companies, Nvidia has no super-voting shares, so after the third incident the board had no choice. Parekh even floats a Jobs-style Jensen return if big institutions push.
items.angle: Governance angle: founder-controlled companies (Meta, Google, Tesla through influence) have the protection Nvidia didn't. It also counts as an underappreciated plus of one-share-one-vote for holders.
items.tweetA: Nvidia's board could push out the most important CEO in the world because Nvidia has no super-voting shares. Meta's board couldn't do that. That cuts both ways for shareholders, and both are now live examples.
items.tweetB: A six-month CEO search in the middle of the Rubin ramp. Every week of interim leadership is a week of decisions made by committee. That's the real cost, and it won't show up in this quarter's numbers.

items.title: Claude Duet reviews: helpful, 'a little neurotic', and still fighting the 'out of sight, out of mind' problem
items.idea: The Verge's review of Anthropic's Claude Duet: it connects to email, calendar, docs and Slack and suggests to-dos you swipe to accept or dismiss; 'a little neurotic and surprisingly helpful.' Parekh, who uses Muse, Instinct and Dots, says the core problem is that he forgets they exist. Agents need to be proactive without being intrusive.
items.angle: The battle among consumer and prosumer agents is about the interaction model, not model quality. Whoever owns the notification layer (phone OS, email client) has the advantage.
items.tweetA: The biggest problem with AI agents isn't capability. It's that users forget they exist. Getting 'proactive without annoying' right is a UX problem worth more than the next model release.
items.tweetB: Swipe to accept a to-do from your AI. Agents are reinventing Tinder for work. Whoever makes that swipe habitual owns the enterprise attention layer.

items.title: MATCH vs RASA: Dylan Patel backs a DUV ban but calls the remote-access bill 'pretty dumb'
items.idea: The MATCH Act would keep advanced DUV lithography (on top of EUV) out of China. RASA would treat remote access to US chips as an export. It passed the House 269-22 in January but is stuck in the Senate and isn't in the NDAA; it covers only frontier-training-sized single-customer clusters, not inference, API access or smuggled chips, and leaves Commerce discretion ('may'). Patel fears Jensen's exit becomes 'cover to pass really stupid laws.'
items.angle: MATCH is the real risk for $ASML, $TEL and $LRCX China revenue. RASA risk falls on Malaysian/SEA neocloud contracts. With Jensen's lobbying gone, the odds of both just rose.
items.tweetA: Jensen was the biggest lobbyist against chip restrictions. He's gone. The MATCH Act (DUV ban to China) just got a lot more likely, and that's an $ASML story, not an $NVDA story.
items.tweetB: RASA passed the House 269-22 and then died in the Senate. That's the mark of a bill nobody wanted to vote against but nobody wanted to pass. Post-Jensen, that changes.

items.title: The case for renting China GPUs: ~$7M Nvidia profit plus $7-10M cloud profit per MW, and a kill switch
items.idea: Patel's game theory: the US goal is maximum lead and maximum control, not zero Chinese compute. A full ban gives China every reason to 'blow up the supply chain' (the largest PCB supplier to Nvidia is Chinese). Rental outside China gives oversight and an off switch, and pays US margin: Nvidia makes ~$7M profit per MW deployed and the cloud provider another $7-10M. Schneider pushes back: Beijing may welcome RASA to force domestic adoption, and China hasn't retaliated on chips since 2022.
items.angle: If rental becomes the main channel, Malaysian/Gulf neoclouds are toll collectors on US-China AI. That's the bull case for RASA staying stalled.
items.tweetA: Every megawatt China rents abroad pays roughly $7M to Nvidia and $7-10M to the cloud. Ban it, and China builds that megawatt at home and keeps the money. Export controls have a revenue line too.
items.tweetB: The largest PCB supplier to Nvidia is Chinese. Every 'cut China off' debate ignores that the US can't build an AI server without Chinese components. Mutually assured supply chains.

items.title: 'Flip the table': control equipment, not chips, and push China up the value chain
items.idea: Patel's framework: removing one item makes China engineer around it (a jigsaw piece), so attack the bottom: 'Don't let them buy ASML equipment... don't let them buy chips, make them rent. Don't let them rent, make them buy the AI.' Nanos: the model capability gap is wider now, but the chip capability gap is 'as close as it's ever been.' Schneider: China broke the 14nm line, but scale (100,000 chips, not 1,000) is the real constraint.
items.angle: Chips are converging while models diverge. This suggests SME (equipment) controls are where policy goes next. That's bearish for Japanese/Dutch equipment exposure to China, bullish for domestic Chinese toolmakers ($Naura, AMEC).
items.tweetA: Chip gap with China: smallest it's ever been. Model gap: wider. So the leverage is in tools, not GPUs. Make China build lithography from scratch. $ASML $TEL
items.tweetB: Capability is a lab result; scale is an industrial result. China can make 1,000 good chips. Making 100,000 needs DUV it can't build yet. That's the whole policy debate in one line.

items.title: China's labs are leaving Nvidia: GLM supports 7 domestic accelerators, DeepSeek wrote an Ascend megakernel
items.idea: SemiAnalysis tracking: GLM launched in February with support for seven domestic accelerators (Huawei, Moore Threads, Hygon, Cambricon, Kunlunxin, MetaX, Enflame). DeepSeek published a megakernel for Huawei Ascend with V4. Meituan says it trained LongCat entirely on Ascend. 'In the US, people don't even train on AMD.'
items.angle: Chinese labs are making their software portable across many chips, while US labs are effectively single-vendor. That's a long-term moat erosion for CUDA in its biggest lost market and a tailwind for Cambricon/Hygon.
items.tweetA: A Chinese open model shipped with support for SEVEN domestic accelerators. US labs barely support two. Portability is turning into China's advantage, and CUDA's moat stops at the border.
items.tweetB: Meituan, a food-delivery company, says it trained a frontier-class model entirely on Huawei Ascend. The 'China can't train without Nvidia' thesis has a shelf life, and it may have just expired.

items.title: US companies make more money serving Chinese open models than the Chinese labs do
items.idea: Patel: application-layer companies running on open models generate 'well north of $10B ARR.' DeepSeek's revenue from V4 Flash is less than what Baseten, Fireworks and other US hosts make serving it. Why no US lab has out-built Kimi or DeepSeek in open weights: 'It's not money. It's talent.' Nvidia spent heavily on Nemotron and still didn't beat Chinese open models.
items.angle: Inference hosts monetize Chinese R&D. A RASA/export escalation that targets Chinese open weights would hurt US inference startups first, and is an underappreciated policy risk for that layer.
items.tweetA: DeepSeek makes less on its own model than the US startups hosting it. China does the R&D, America collects the inference revenue. The best trade in the US-China AI race may be the toll booth.
items.tweetB: Nvidia spent billions on Nemotron and still couldn't beat Kimi or DeepSeek in open models. If money can't buy the open frontier, the bottleneck is talent, and US policy toward Chinese researchers is the real AI policy.

items.title: Nvidia's execution risk: Rubin yields, Feynman timing, and the 70% of supply chain that showed up because Jensen asked
items.idea: Patel: Jensen made the decision to add Tensor Cores to Volta three months before tape-out. Without '100 of those decisions,' Feynman could be worse and later, Rubin's yield ramp slower, Rubin Ultra may slip, and the supply chain may stop giving Nvidia ~70% of capacity 'because it's Jensen asking.' By 2029 the best chips may not be Nvidia's. Also: Nvidia no longer reports Singapore revenue. Nanos counters that short-term Nvidia is fine, citing Apple after 2011.
items.angle: The risk is a 2028-29 roadmap slip, not this quarter. That favors $AVGO custom silicon and $AMD at the margin, and TSMC allocation power shifts to whoever asks next.
items.tweetA: Volta got Tensor Cores three months before tape-out because Jensen overruled his engineers. That one call basically started the AI era. Committees don't make calls like that. $NVDA $AVGO
items.tweetB: TSMC reportedly gave Nvidia ~70% of capacity because Jensen personally asked. That allocation was a relationship, not a contract. Who inherits it is the quiet question of 2027. $TSM

items.title: Talent flight risk: 'the sharks are in the water' for Nvidia's EVPs and VPs
items.idea: Nanos: Jensen was extraordinarily good at retention; almost no high-profile executive departures (only Rene Haas left to run Arm). Now VCs will offer people 'billions of dollars' to start chip companies and neolabs. A year from now, a wave of departures would be a red flag. He adds that finance (Kress) is now in charge, so expect high near-term profitability and a very different company in the medium term.
items.angle: Any 13F-style tracking of Nvidia SVP departures to startups is the key 12-month leading indicator. A spin-out wave is also a venture-funding theme for 2027.
items.tweetA: Nvidia's executive team almost never left. That was Jensen's quietest achievement. Every VC in the Valley is now dialing Santa Clara. Track LinkedIn, not earnings calls.
items.tweetB: When finance takes over from the founder, the next few quarters are the most profitable in company history, and then the roadmap thins out. Ask Intel how 2005-2015 went.

items.title: Contrarian: why would Beijing plant a spy to import chips it's telling Alibaba not to buy?
items.idea: The author argues the spy claim rests on anonymous US intelligence sources with no evidence shown. Jensen says Nvidia's China share of advanced chips fell from 95% to 0% after export controls, a big incentive to get around them. Beijing has spent billions on domestic chips, pushed Alibaba to buy local and opened an antitrust case against Nvidia. So a spy smuggling Nvidia chips in would be working against Beijing's own policy. More likely, Alice Huang was a smuggler working against both governments.
items.angle: Parekh hints at the same thing (some agencies are 'retreating' from the spy claim). If the spy story collapses and it becomes a pure export-violation case, the legal tail is contained, but so is any chance of a Jensen comeback.
items.tweetA: The question no one asks: why would China send a spy to bring in Nvidia chips while it pushes its own companies to buy Huawei? The 'spy' story makes less sense than the 'smuggler' story. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Nvidia's China share went from 95% to 0%. Put that much money behind a border and someone always builds a tunnel. That's not espionage; that's economics doing what it always does.

items.title: Microsoft's 12-hour global outage: Japan went back to fax, UK police went back to phones
items.idea: Microsoft's outage lasted 12+ hours, hit ~20 services (Outlook, Teams) and users in 70+ countries; Microsoft says technical failure, not cyber or AI. Japanese organizations used fax machines; UK police told people to phone in crimes. The argument: a second cloud is an incomplete continuity plan if failover instructions arrive via Outlook. The real resilience criterion is independence. Microsoft was also reported (Nov 9) to be winding down a 2023 Oracle compute-capacity deal.
items.angle: Resilience spend shifts to out-of-band comms and multi-vendor identity ($OKTA, $CRWD tangentially). For $MSFT the reputational cost lands right as it sells Copilot as essential infrastructure.
items.tweetA: Microsoft went down for 12 hours in 70 countries and Japan's answer was the fax machine. The most resilient tech in the world is the one nobody bothered to migrate. $MSFT
items.tweetB: Your failover plan says 'switch to the backup cloud.' The instructions for switching arrive in Outlook. Outlook is down. That's the whole problem with single-vendor resilience in one sentence.

items.title: Turkey and Qatar sign a mutual defense agreement
items.idea: According to the Turkish presidency, Turkey and Qatar signed a mutual defense agreement, noted among the news items in The Pressure Point while the Iran war status quo continues.
items.angle: A NATO member formally tied to defending a Gulf state that hosts Al Udeid and has Iran ties is a new kind of security link in the Gulf. That bears on Hormuz risk pricing and LNG (Qatar is a top exporter).
items.tweetA: A NATO member just signed a mutual defense pact with Qatar, the world's #2 LNG exporter, in the middle of an Iran war. Gulf security is no longer just a US guarantee. $LNG
items.tweetB: Turkey now has defense commitments stretching from the Baltic (via NATO) to the Gulf. Ankara is quietly becoming the swing military power of the region.

items.title: FAA issues a rare nationwide ground stop on all departing flights
items.idea: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA issued a rare nationwide ground stop covering all departing flights on Friday, the same day as the global Microsoft outage.
items.angle: Two nationwide infrastructure failures in one day (cloud and air traffic) push resilience spending up the agenda. Airline Q4 numbers may take a hit from the disruption.
items.tweetA: Microsoft down globally and the FAA grounding every departing flight in the US, on Friday the 13th. Infrastructure fragility isn't a tail risk anymore; it's a weekly event. $UAL $DAL
items.tweetB: A nationwide FAA ground stop used to happen after a terror attack. Now it happens after a systems failure. That's the cost of decades of underinvestment in air traffic control.

items.title: Boebert loses a deep-red Colorado seat; Van Hollen challenges Schumer
items.idea: Democrat Eileen Laubacher defeated Rep. Lauren Boebert in a deep-red Colorado district, flipping a House seat. Sen. Chris Van Hollen says he'll challenge Chuck Schumer for Democratic Senate leadership. ChinaTalk mentions the Iran war cost Trump '10 Senate seats.'
items.angle: A blue wave raises the odds of 2027+ antitrust and M&A friction (see TWiST's 'race to close deals'), more aggressive export policy, and fiscal gridlock.
items.tweetA: Boebert losing a deep-red seat isn't a local story. It's the signal that the 2026 wave was broad, and dealmakers just got a 6-12 month window to close before Washington changes.
items.tweetB: A leadership challenge to Schumer from the left after a winning election means the incoming Democratic majority wants a fight, not compromise. Price more policy volatility in 2027, not less.

items.title: Industrials losing ground to the equal-weight S&P: 'hiking into deceleration'
items.idea: Tavi Costa watches industrials vs the equal-weight S&P 500 as a read on economic health. If they keep underperforming, a slower-growth period is likely, which could force 'pretty drastic changes in monetary policy.' His bigger worry is the Fed hiking into that slowdown.
items.angle: This conflicts with the Boockvar/Ferguson/Cummins data showing strong industrial order books, so this is a market-price vs fundamentals divergence worth watching. Hiking into deceleration is the classic setup that comes before a policy reversal, which would mean a steeper curve.
items.tweetA: Industrials vs equal-weight S&P is rolling over while the Fed talks about 50bp hikes. Hiking into a slowdown is how you get an emergency cut 9 months later. $XLI $RSP
items.tweetB: Cummins and Ferguson report strong data center orders, yet industrials as a group are underperforming the equal-weight index. The market is looking past AI capex to the old economy, and it doesn't like what it sees.

charts.desc: Industrials relative to equal-weighted S&P 500, rolling over. Chart inside, worth opening.

items.title: $2K per employee on AI tools, and Ro's 12x revenue growth with flat headcount
items.idea: Jason Calacanis spends $2K per employee per year on AI tools and would double it; making a $100K employee just 1% more efficient pays for it. Ro's annualized run rate went from $250M in 2021 to nearly $3B today with team size roughly unchanged.
items.angle: Revenue per employee is becoming the KPI. This is a structural headwind for white-collar hiring (consistent with 'low hire, low fire') and a tailwind for SaaS seats priced as AI tools.
items.tweetA: Ro went from $250M to ~$3B in run rate with the same headcount. That's 12x revenue per employee in five years. Watch the 'low hire' labor market for the cause. $HIMS
items.tweetB: $2,000 of AI tooling per worker pays for itself at a 1% productivity gain on a $100K salary. That math is why enterprise AI spend keeps growing even when the stocks don't.

items.title: HubSpot brings its founder back after a 75% five-year drawdown: the 'refounding' playbook
items.idea: After its stock lost 75% in five years, HubSpot became the latest company to bring back its founder CEO and try 'refounding.' Calacanis: a founder makes bold moves without always looking over their shoulder, unlike a hired-gun CEO.
items.angle: The timing is a nice contrast: Nvidia just lost its founder while HubSpot reinstates one. Founder-return situations (Starbucks, Apple) historically produce big re-ratings, and SaaS companies hit by AI fears are the candidate pool.
items.tweetA: HubSpot brings back its founder after a 75% drawdown. Nvidia loses its founder at the top. Same week, opposite directions. The market will tell us which matters more: founders or moats. $HUBS $NVDA
items.tweetB: AI is forcing every SaaS company to rebuild its product. Hired managers optimize; founders rebuild. Expect more 'refoundings' across the SaaS 2021 cohort.

items.title: 'Race to close deals' in the next 6-12 months before Democrats retake power
items.idea: Calacanis says the industry is in a 'race to close deals' over the next 6-12 months, before Democrats retake power in Washington and shut M&A down.
items.angle: An M&A window with a deadline means front-loaded deal volume in H1 2027, which supports $GS/$MS advisory and merger-arb spreads that should tighten for deals that can close fast.
items.tweetA: Dealmakers think they have 6-12 months before Washington shuts M&A down again. A deadline-driven deal rush is great for bankers and dangerous for overpaying acquirers. $GS $MS
items.tweetB: Every 'get it done before the regime changes' wave in M&A has ended with deals that looked expensive in hindsight. Urgency is not a valuation method.

items.title: DXY ends the week at its highest level since April 2025
items.idea: The US Dollar Index rose sharply over the past week and went into the weekend at its highest since April 2025, after Waller's 50bp talk and the hawkish front-end move.
items.angle: A strong dollar plus a Fed hiking plus Japan's inflation impulse is a recipe for EM stress and pressure on USD-denominated commodities. Also a headwind for gold and BTC (which is already below $70k).
items.tweetA: Dollar at its highest since April 2025. Bitcoin below $70k. Gold struggling. When the Fed talks hikes, the dollar is the only thing that works, and that's the most crowded macro trade there is. $DXY $UUP
items.tweetB: A 19-month high in DXY lands right as US multinationals guide 2027. Every 5% of dollar strength is roughly 1-2% off S&P EPS. The EPS peak argument just got a currency tailwind, against it.

charts.desc: DXY daily chart (Koyfin) at highest since Apr'25.

items.title: SMH -25% and XLK -15% from highs, yet SPY is only 3% down; every prior case saw a double-digit SPY drawdown
items.idea: In the five prior episodes since 2011 when SMH was 25%+ and XLK 15%+ below their 52-week highs, SPY was already in a double-digit drawdown every time. Today SPY is down just 3%.
items.angle: Either 2026 really is different (broad earnings, rotation into healthcare and staples, as Innes says) or the index is lagging. An RSP-vs-SPY pair or SPY put spreads cheaply express the second view.
items.tweetA: Five times since 2011, semis fell 25% and tech 15%. Every single time, the S&P was already down double digits. This time it's down 3%. Either the rest of the market has never been stronger, or it hasn't noticed yet. $SPY $SMH
items.tweetB: The index has never ignored a semis drawdown like this. The bull case is a rotation into staples, healthcare and the 495. The bear case is that 5-for-5 is a pretty good track record.

charts.desc: Table/chart of SMH/XLK drawdown episodes vs SPY drawdown since 2011.

items.title: Top 5 vs bottom 495 valuation premium is the tightest in almost 10 years
items.idea: Goldman Sachs (via @mikezaccardi): the valuation premium of the largest US companies over the rest 'has narrowed... tightest in almost 10 years.' The ICYMI section also flags that credit spreads on hyperscalers and big chip companies 'have blown out.'
items.angle: Mega-cap equity premiums are compressing while their credit spreads widen. That's the AI capex financing cost showing up in both places, and a reason to look at the 495 for quality.
items.tweetA: The mega-cap valuation premium is the tightest in a decade, and hyperscaler credit spreads just blew out. The market is charging Big Tech for its capex for the first time. $MSFT $META $GOOGL
items.tweetB: Everyone spent three years asking when the Mag 7 premium would close. It's closing now, through the top coming down rather than the 495 catching up. Careful what you wish for.

charts.desc: Goldman: top 5 vs remaining 495 forward P/E premium, narrowest in ~10 years.

items.title: S&P Q3 EPS growth at 31.9%: 3rd straight quarter above 25%, 8th straight double-digit
items.idea: FactSet: with 91% of the S&P 500 reported, the blended Q3 YoY growth rate is 31.9%, the 3rd straight quarter of 25%+ and the 8th straight quarter of double-digit growth. The market is also punishing negative EPS surprises less than average.
items.angle: 31.9% EPS growth with the index flat since June means multiples are compressing fast, which is what a rising-rate regime looks like. Earnings are strong; the discount rate is winning.
items.tweetA: S&P EPS growth: 31.9% y/y. Index: flat since June. That isn't a weak market, it's multiple compression from rates eating every dollar of earnings growth. $SPY
items.tweetB: Eight straight double-digit quarters of earnings growth and the Fed is hiking. Nominal growth is booming. That's not a recession setup; it's an inflation setup. The bond market got the memo first.

charts.desc: FactSet S&P 500 quarterly EPS growth bars.

items.title: Timmer: forward EPS estimates +39% y/y against 19% expected growth; peak earnings growth via base effects
items.idea: Fidelity's Jurrien Timmer: 'One question is whether we have finally reached peak earnings growth. It's starting to look that way.' Next-12-month EPS estimates are up 39% y/y but look 'toppy' against expected growth of 19% over the next year as the base effect kicks in.
items.angle: Earnings growth decelerating from 39% to 19% while rates rise is the classic second-derivative headwind for growth multiples. Combined with the DXY rally, 2027 EPS revisions are the risk.
items.tweetA: Forward EPS +39% y/y, expected growth next year 19%. Growth halving while the Fed hikes. Markets trade the second derivative, and the second derivative just turned. $SPY $QQQ
items.tweetB: Peak earnings growth plus peak dollar plus peak Fed hawkishness rarely happen all at once. When they do, it usually marks the middle of a cycle, not the end. Whether it's a pause or a top depends on credit spreads.

charts.desc: Fidelity (Timmer): S&P n12m EPS estimate y/y vs expected growth, rolling over.
